title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Tonight: Lyon Twp residents voice grid and road fears ahead of next month's hearing.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're zeroing in on Lyon Township in Oakland County, where a data center developer is heading back before planners next month amid fresh resident pushback over power and roads.
That sounds like the tip of a much bigger iceberg, Graham. What's the latest on this Lyon project specifically?

The developer is scheduled for another appearance before Lyon Township planners next month. Locals have already flagged worries about how much power the facility would pull from the grid and the extra traffic it could dump on local roads.
How does this fit into the wider pattern we've seen popping up all over the state this week?

It's the same story repeating itself. Communities from Washtenaw to Tuscola to Genesee are suddenly dealing with proposals that could reshape their power bills, water supplies, and even local farmland.
Walk me through why power demand is such a flashpoint here.

These facilities are huge electricity users. One of the stories we saw this week ties directly into DTE's big rate-hike request, and Attorney General Nessel is pushing to slash that increase by 71 percent because households would feel it hard.
So even if the data center brings jobs, the cost could land on regular ratepayers?
Exactly. The AG called out data center demand as one factor behind the $474 million ask. A smaller hike still means higher bills, but the full amount would hit especially tough.
What about water use? We've heard that concern in a couple places already.
The million-construction-hour milestone at the big Ann Arbor-area project has Washtenaw residents asking the same questions. Once these places ramp up, how much water will they need for cooling?
And farmland is getting converted fast too, right?

Look at Saline Township. The project nicknamed The Barn is rising quickly on what used to be farmland. Neighbors are already seeing new power lines going in and wondering about traffic and tax shifts.
Taxes seem like another hidden piece. How transparent are these deals?

Michigan law lets companies keep the details of their tax breaks secret from the public and even local officials. That means towns and cities can lose revenue without residents knowing the full picture.
So if one township gives a big abatement, does that mean higher taxes or fewer services for everybody else?
That's the worry. When big facilities arrive with abatements, the revenue gap can show up as higher local taxes or strained services for people living 30 miles away.
What's the next concrete step in Lyon?
The hearing next month. Residents will get another chance to speak directly to planners about the grid strain and road impacts before any big decisions.
Are other townships taking similar pauses or tightening rules?
Yes. Ellington Township just approved a moratorium to give locals time to study power, water, and tax effects. Wixom is moving new restrictions even as a lawsuit threat grows from developers.
And Madison Heights just got its first formal site plan filing.
That's right. First concrete step in that Oakland County suburb, and people nearby are already thinking about what it could mean for their power lines and water systems.
Genesee County also got an impact study delivered this week.
A local committee finished its report on power, water, and road strain and handed it to leaders. Officials now have numbers to work with before any projects advance.
Lawmakers are also stepping in at the state level.
New bills introduced this week would add rules on power use, noise, and tax deals for large data centers. It's a direct response to the community pushback we've been tracking.
So the Lyon hearing next month could be a test case for how these new rules might play out locally?
It could. Planners there will have to weigh the same issues that are driving the state legislation and the moratoriums elsewhere.
What happens if residents keep showing up and raising these points?
It can slow things down or force changes. We've seen that pattern in Wixom and Ellington already this week.
Any sense of how many communities are now actively looking at this?
At least a half-dozen townships and cities have taken some action or held hearings in the past week alone. The map is lighting up fast.
Back to Lyon for a second — any details on the size or timeline of that specific project?
Not much beyond the fact that it's big enough to trigger these grid and road concerns. The next hearing should bring more specifics out into the open.
All right, let's shift to quick hits. First up, that construction milestone near Ann Arbor.
The project hit one million construction hours. Washtenaw residents are now watching closely for long-term effects on electricity rates and water once operations start.
And in Saline Township?
The Barn is moving quickly on farmland. Neighbors expect new power lines, more traffic, and possible tax changes as it comes online.
Madison Heights filed its first site plan on Sunday.
Yes, the first formal step in that Oakland County suburb. Effects could ripple to power and water systems for residents nearby.
Wixom is tightening rules while facing a lawsuit threat.
Officials advanced new restrictions on data centers despite the looming legal pushback from developers.
Ellington Township approved a moratorium on Saturday.
Residents there secured a pause so the board can study power demands, water use, and tax effects before any projects move forward.
Genesee panel delivered its impact study.
The committee submitted details on potential strain to power, water, and roads for local leaders to review.
And the AG's push on DTE's rate hike.
Dana Nessel wants regulators to cut the $474 million request by 71 percent, citing data center demand as one driver.
Finally, the new state bills targeting big builds.
Lawmakers introduced measures for tighter oversight on power, noise, and tax incentives across Michigan.
Now, on deck — what meetings can listeners actually attend soon?
Mark your calendars for the Lyon Township planners meeting next month. That's where the data center developer returns and residents can speak directly on grid and road concerns.
Any other upcoming sessions we should flag?
Wixom continues its work on new restrictions, and several other townships are still reviewing their own moratorium or study options. Check your local clerk for exact dates.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Lyon Township Hearing Looms as Data Center Worries Spread Across Michigan
